processing: Leaves are blanched, rolled, packed into bamboo tubes or clay jars, sealed with banana leaf and buried to ferment for one to ten months, judged by experience rather than instruments.
harvest_season: Spring and summer picking from old tea trees, taking a bud with three or four leaves.
appearance_dry: Not a dry tea in the usual sense: a dense, moist mass of dark, soft fermented leaf, as is typical of pickled teas.
appearance_liquor: Little is documented about an infusion, since it is mainly eaten; expect a pale, dull amber if it is steeped, as with other fermented leaf.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark olive-brown leaves that have lost their spring and hold together in clumps.
taste_profile: Sour and tea-bitter, as the name and the long buried fermentation suggest; detailed tasting notes for this tea are scarce.

brewing.notes: Normally chewed or eaten as a food rather than brewed. If you steep a pinch, treat it as an experiment; there is no established brewing method.

vintage_note: Made in small household batches and rarely sold as a graded commercial tea, so there are no recognised vintages or seasons on the market. A batch is ready after its months underground and is usually eaten locally.
description:
Bulang sour tea is less a drink than a food: tea leaf pickled by the Bulang people of southern Yunnan and eaten. It belongs to the same family as the pickled teas of Southeast Asia, and it has little to do with what you would normally put in a gaiwan.

The method is simple and slow. Leaf from old trees is blanched and rolled, packed into bamboo or clay, closed with banana leaf and buried, then left for anywhere from a month to ten months. Timing and conditions rest on the maker's experience.

The point is sourness alongside the bitterness of the leaf. Few detailed tasting descriptions exist, and most accounts focus on how it is made rather than how each batch differs, so approach it without fixed expectations.

You are unlikely to find it in a tea shop. If you meet it, it will probably be homemade, in a village around Menghai or Jingmai, and that is the best way to try it. Do not confuse it with the sour tea of the De'ang people, a separate tradition with its own national heritage listing.
history: Little is firmly documented. Popular accounts place its origin on Jingmai Mountain and tell a legend involving the Bulang leader Ba Leng, explaining fermentation as a way to keep tea; treat this as legend. A travel account also records people seeking suancha among Bulang villagers near Nannuo Mountain in Menghai, which shows it survives as a living local food. No reliable dating of the practice is available.
